explain: XGBoost is the SageMaker built-in algorithm designed for tabular data with gradient-boosted trees for regression and classification. DeepAR targets time series and BlazingText targets text.
options: XGBoost gradient-boosted trees for tabular classification and regression tasks
DeepAR recurrent network for probabilistic multi-series time-series forecasting
BlazingText Word2Vec and text classifier for large-scale natural language corpora
K-Means unsupervised clustering that assigns each record to one of K cluster groups
q: A bank wants to predict loan defaults from tabular customer features. Which SageMaker built-in algorithm fits best?

explain: Linear Learner trains linear models for regression and binary or multiclass classification on tabular data. K-Means clusters unlabeled data and DeepAR forecasts time series instead.
options: K-Means clustering that groups unlabeled records into K clusters by feature similarity
Linear Learner for large-scale linear regression and linear classification model training
DeepAR autoregressive RNN that produces probabilistic forecasts for many related series
BlazingText scalable Word2Vec embedding and text classification for document collections
q: Which SageMaker built-in algorithm trains linear regression and linear classification models at scale?

explain: DeepAR is the SageMaker built-in algorithm for probabilistic forecasting across many related time series. XGBoost handles tabular data and Object Detection finds objects in images.
options: XGBoost, which trains gradient-boosted trees on tabular rows for regression and classification
Linear Learner, which fits linear regression and classification models on numeric feature vectors
DeepAR recurrent network for probabilistic forecasting of many related time-series streams
Object Detection, a Single Shot Detector that predicts bounding boxes plus labels in images
q: A retailer needs probabilistic demand forecasts for thousands of product sales histories. Which algorithm should it use?

explain: BlazingText implements Word2Vec embeddings and text classification at scale. Factorization Machines target sparse recommendation data, not text embeddings.
options: DeepAR probabilistic forecaster that learns seasonal patterns from many related time series
K-Means unsupervised method that partitions records into K groups by distance in feature space
Factorization Machines model for sparse click-through and recommendation data with pairwise interactions
BlazingText for scalable Word2Vec embeddings and fast supervised text classification tasks
q: A team needs fast Word2Vec embeddings and text classification on millions of documents. Which algorithm fits?

explain: K-Means is the unsupervised clustering algorithm that partitions unlabeled records into K groups. Linear Learner and XGBoost are supervised and need labeled targets.
options: K-Means clustering that partitions unlabeled customer records into K distinct behavior segments
Linear Learner regression that fits a linear model to labeled numeric targets on tabular data
XGBoost classifier that trains boosted trees on labeled rows for binary or multiclass outcomes
Factorization Machines recommender that learns pairwise interactions from sparse click matrices
q: A marketing team wants to segment unlabeled customers into groups by behavior. Which algorithm should it choose?

explain: Factorization Machines are built for sparse, high-dimensional data such as clicks and recommendations. Object Detection works on images, not sparse user-item matrices.
options: Object Detection SSD that predicts labeled bounding boxes around objects visible inside images
Factorization Machines for click-through prediction on sparse high-dimensional interaction data
Semantic Segmentation FCN that assigns a class label to every single pixel of an input image
Linear Learner optimizer that trains linear regression models on dense tabular numeric features
q: Which SageMaker built-in algorithm is designed for sparse click-through and recommendation problems?

explain: The Object Detection algorithm (Single Shot Detector) predicts bounding boxes and class labels in images. Semantic Segmentation instead labels every pixel rather than drawing boxes.
options: K-Means clustering that assigns image feature vectors to K groups without any bounding boxes
Semantic Segmentation FCN that classifies every pixel of an image into a semantic category map
Object Detection SSD that locates objects with bounding boxes plus class labels in images
BlazingText classifier that labels whole text documents using learned word embedding vectors
q: A warehouse needs to locate boxes in photos with bounding boxes and labels. Which built-in algorithm fits?

explain: Semantic Segmentation labels every pixel of an image, which is exactly what road-scene segmentation needs. Object Detection only draws boxes and K-Means only clusters records.
options: Object Detection SSD that draws one bounding box with a label around each visible object
K-Means clustering that groups whole images into K clusters by overall feature similarity
Image Classification classifier that assigns a single topic label to each entire input image
Semantic Segmentation FCN that assigns a class label to every pixel of the input image
q: An autonomous-driving team must label every pixel of road scenes (road, car, pedestrian). Which algorithm fits?

explain: JumpStart provides pre-trained foundation models and prebuilt solutions deployable in SageMaker with a few clicks. Training Jobs instead run fully custom training code from scratch.
options: SageMaker JumpStart with pre-trained foundation models and ready-made solutions for quick deployment
SageMaker Training Jobs that run fully custom training scripts on managed compute infrastructure
SageMaker Autopilot that automatically tries preprocessing, algorithms, and tuning for tabular data
SageMaker Experiments tracker that versions datasets, parameters, and metrics across training runs
q: A startup wants to deploy a pre-trained foundation model with minimal effort. Which SageMaker capability fits best?

explain: SageMaker Autopilot automates the full tabular ML pipeline: preprocessing, algorithm selection, and hyperparameter tuning, then ranks candidates. JumpStart deploys prebuilt models instead.
options: SageMaker JumpStart catalog that deploys pre-trained foundation models and prebuilt ML solutions
SageMaker Autopilot, which automates preprocessing, algorithm choice, and tuning for tabular data
SageMaker Debugger, which monitors tensors during training to flag vanishing gradients or overfit
SageMaker Profiler, which profiles GPU, CPU, and data-loading bottlenecks in deep learning jobs
q: A business analyst with no ML expertise needs a baseline classifier from a CSV. Which no-code AutoML option fits?

explain: A SageMaker Training Job runs user code on managed infrastructure, supports distributed training and Managed Spot Training. Autopilot is the automated no-code alternative for tabular data.
options: SageMaker Autopilot run that automatically engineers features and tunes models for tabular CSV data
SageMaker JumpStart solution that deploys a pre-trained model or template with minimal coding effort
SageMaker Training Job on managed infrastructure with distributed and Managed Spot Training support
SageMaker Experiments trial that records parameters, datasets, and metrics to compare model versions
q: A team wants to train custom PyTorch code on managed GPUs. Which SageMaker capability should it use?

explain: Automatic Model Tuning searches hyperparameters with Bayesian optimization and returns the best configuration. Debugger monitors training tensors rather than searching hyperparameters.
options: SageMaker Debugger monitor that inspects gradients and activations during training to catch anomalies
SageMaker Profiler tool that measures hardware utilization and data pipeline bottlenecks in training
SageMaker Experiments tracker that organizes trials, artifacts, and metrics to compare model versions
Automatic Model Tuning, which uses Bayesian search over hyperparameters to find the best configuration
q: Which SageMaker feature automatically searches hyperparameters to find the best model configuration?

explain: Precision is true positives over all predicted positives, so it measures false-alarm rate. Recall instead measures how many actual positives were found.
options: Precision: the share of predicted positives that are truly positive, penalizing false alarms
Recall: the share of actual positives the model found, penalizing missed positive cases
Accuracy: the share of all predictions that are correct across every class in the dataset
RMSE: the square root of averaged squared errors, penalizing large regression mistakes heavily
q: A spam filter must minimize false alarms on legitimate email. Which metric should the team prioritize?

explain: Recall measures the fraction of real positives detected, so it fits screening where missing a case is costly. Precision instead focuses on false alarms among predicted positives.
options: Precision metric that rewards few false alarms among the cases the model flags as positive
Recall, the fraction of actual positive cases the model successfully detects and flags
F1 score, the harmonic mean that balances precision and recall into one single number
AUC-ROC, the ranking score computed over all classification thresholds of the model curve
q: A disease-screening model must miss as few true cases as possible. Which metric matters most?

explain: Overfitting means low training error but high validation error, so regularization or more data helps. Underfitting instead shows high error on both training and validation sets.
options: Underfitting, where both training and validation errors stay high because the model is too simple
Well-calibrated fitting, where training and validation errors are both low and closely aligned
Overfitting: low training error but high validation error, fixed with regularization or more data
Converged optimization, where the loss curve flattens because the learning rate decayed to zero
q: Training error is near zero but validation error is very high. What is happening and what helps?

explain: Managed Spot Training uses spare EC2 capacity with checkpointing so interrupted jobs resume, cutting costs up to 70%. On-Demand instances never get interrupted but cost the full price.
options: On-Demand ml.p3 instances that run without interruption but bill the full hourly compute price
Reserved Savings Plan capacity that lowers price in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment
SageMaker Profiler sessions that optimize GPU kernels but leave the instance billing rate unchanged
Managed Spot Training with checkpointing, using spare capacity to cut costs despite interruptions
q: A team trains fault-tolerant models for many hours and must minimize compute cost. Which SageMaker option fits?

explain: Data-parallel training replicates the model on each worker with synchronized gradients, scaling batch size. Model parallel instead splits a too-large model across devices.
options: Data-parallel training that replicates the model on workers and synchronizes gradients each step
Model-parallel sharding that splits model layers across devices when one GPU cannot hold them
Sequential single-GPU training that processes every batch on one device without any parallelism
Spot-instance checkpointing that saves state to S3 so interrupted training jobs can resume later
q: A CNN fits on one GPU but training is too slow on a large dataset. Which distributed strategy should apply first?

explain: Experiments tracks trials, parameters, datasets, and metrics so runs are comparable and reproducible. Debugger inspects live tensors while Profiler measures hardware utilization.
options: SageMaker Debugger hook that inspects live gradients and weights to catch training anomalies early
SageMaker Experiments, which tracks datasets, parameters, and metrics to compare training runs
SageMaker Profiler report that breaks down GPU, CPU, and data-loader time across training steps
SageMaker Model Registry entry that versions approved models and controls production promotion steps
q: After dozens of runs nobody can reproduce the best score. Which SageMaker feature restores reproducibility?

explain: Debugger inspects tensors such as gradients and activations during training and raises alerts on anomalies. Profiler measures system utilization rather than tensor values.
options: SageMaker Profiler timeline that measures GPU utilization and input pipeline stalls during training
SageMaker Experiments lineage that records which dataset and parameters produced each trained model
SageMaker Debugger, which inspects training tensors and alerts on issues like vanishing gradients
Automatic Model Tuning job that searches hyperparameters with Bayesian optimization across trials
q: Loss stops improving and gradients may be vanishing. Which SageMaker tool diagnoses the training internals?

explain: Profiler identifies hardware and pipeline bottlenecks such as low GPU utilization or slow data loading. Debugger instead watches tensor values like gradients for training anomalies.
options: SageMaker Debugger rule that watches gradient norms and weight updates to flag training pathologies
Automatic Model Tuning search that evaluates hyperparameter combinations ranked by validation score
SageMaker Experiments comparison that aligns metrics and parameters across many recorded trials
SageMaker Profiler, which pinpoints GPU underuse and data-loading bottlenecks in training jobs
q: GPUs sit idle while the data pipeline lags. Which SageMaker tool pinpoints the bottleneck?

explain: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, ideal for imbalanced classes where accuracy misleads. Accuracy can look high by always predicting the majority class.
options: F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall suited to imbalanced classification tasks
Accuracy, the overall fraction correct that looks deceptively high on strongly skewed datasets
RMSE, the root of mean squared error used for regression rather than class prediction tasks
Log-loss, the probabilistic penalty that also needs calibrated scores, not just hard labels
q: Fraud data is 99% legitimate, so accuracy looks great while fraud is missed. Which metric should lead instead?

explain: RMSE squares errors before averaging, so large mistakes dominate it, while MAE weights all errors linearly. Teams pick RMSE when big misses are especially costly.
options: MAE averages absolute errors linearly, so every unit of error counts equally regardless of size
RMSE squares errors before averaging, punishing a few large misses far more than small ones
R-squared reports explained variance as a ratio, hiding the absolute scale of prediction errors
MAPE divides errors by actuals, becoming unstable whenever true values approach zero levels
q: Two regression models have similar MAE, but one makes rare huge errors. Which metric exposes that difference?

explain: AUC-ROC measures ranking quality across all thresholds, independent of any single cutoff. Accuracy and F1 both depend on one chosen threshold.
options: Accuracy at a fixed cutoff, which hides ranking quality and shifts whenever the threshold moves
F1 at one tuned threshold, which reflects a single operating point rather than overall ranking
AUC-ROC, which measures ranking quality across all thresholds independent of any cutoff choice
Log-loss at fixed calibration, which penalizes probability errors but not pure ordering directly
q: A team compares classifiers independent of any decision threshold. Which metric measures overall ranking quality?

explain: K-fold cross-validation averages performance over K held-out folds, reducing split luck and revealing variance. A single split can look good or bad by chance.
options: A single train-test split, which is fast but lets one lucky or unlucky partition decide the score
A larger test set alone, which shrinks noise but still evaluates only one fixed data partition
Repeated training on the full data, which reuses the same rows and cannot estimate generalization
K-fold cross-validation, averaging scores over K held-out folds to reduce split luck and variance
q: With a small dataset, a single split gives unstable scores. Which evaluation approach is more reliable?

explain: Early stopping halts training when validation loss stops improving, keeping the best checkpoint. It prevents the extra epochs from fitting noise in the training set.
options: Early stopping that halts training when validation loss stalls and keeps the best checkpoint
Longer training that continues epochs after validation stalls, fitting noise in training data
Higher learning rates that overshoot minima and make validation loss oscillate or diverge
Stronger augmentation alone that expands data variety but never decides when to stop training
q: Validation loss improves, then worsens while training loss keeps falling. What should the team do?

explain: Log-loss penalizes confident wrong probabilities, so it suits decisions needing calibrated risk scores. Accuracy only counts hard labels and ignores confidence entirely.
options: Accuracy counting hard labels, which ignores how confident or calibrated each prediction was
Log-loss, which penalizes confident wrong probabilities and rewards well-calibrated risk scores
MAE on class indices, which treats labels as ordered numbers and misreads classification error
RMSE on one-hot vectors, which distorts probability error with an inappropriate regression scale
q: A credit-risk model must output calibrated default probabilities, not just labels. Which loss fits model selection?

explain: Underfitting shows high error on both training and validation data, calling for more capacity or features. Regularization would shrink capacity further and worsen it.
options: Overfitting pattern, where training error is low but validation error stays high from excess capacity
Label leakage pattern, where validation scores look unrealistically perfect due to future information
Underfitting: high error on both training and validation, needing more capacity or better features
Convergence noise pattern, where both curves oscillate because the learning rate is set too high
q: Both training and validation errors are high with a tiny linear model. What is wrong and what helps?

explain: Autopilot builds preprocessing plus algorithm pipelines automatically and returns ranked candidates with leaderboards. AMT only tunes hyperparameters of a user-defined setup.
options: Automatic Model Tuning search that optimizes hyperparameters for one user-defined training setup
SageMaker Debugger monitor that watches live tensors to flag gradient or convergence anomalies
JumpStart fine-tuning flow that adapts a chosen foundation model with custom labeled examples
Autopilot, which builds preprocessing plus algorithm pipelines and ranks candidates automatically
q: A team wants automated feature preprocessing plus a ranked leaderboard of models. Which option delivers that?

explain: Bayesian optimization models the objective from past trials and samples promising regions, beating grid and random search efficiency. Grid search wastes budget on unpromising areas.
options: Bayesian optimization, which models past trial results to sample the most promising hyperparameters
Exhaustive grid search, which evaluates every combination even in regions already known to be poor
Manual trial-and-error, which depends on engineer intuition and rarely covers the space systematically
Single default training, which accepts preset hyperparameters without exploring any alternatives
q: Why does SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning prefer Bayesian search over exhaustive grid search?

explain: L1 and L2 penalties plus dropout constrain capacity and reduce overfitting. Adding layers or training longer would increase overfitting instead.
options: Adding hidden layers and training longer, which grows capacity and memorizes training noise further
Regularization such as L1, L2, or dropout that constrains capacity and curbs memorization of noise
Removing validation monitoring, which blinds the team while the model keeps overfitting silently
Shrinking the dataset sharply, which leaves fewer examples and makes memorization even easier
q: A deep network memorizes training data with a large generalization gap. Which remedy should the team apply?

explain: MAE averages absolute errors so it stays robust to a few huge outliers. RMSE would amplify those outliers through squaring and misrepresent typical accuracy.
options: RMSE objective that squares each error, letting a handful of huge outliers dominate the score
R-squared ranking that reports explained variance but obscures the absolute size of typical errors
MAE, which averages absolute errors linearly and stays robust when a few huge outliers exist
MAPE percentage that divides by actuals and becomes unstable whenever true values near zero
q: Delivery-time data has a few extreme outliers, and typical error matters most. Which regression metric fits?

explain: JumpStart solutions bundle models, notebooks, and infrastructure templates for common use cases. Training Jobs run custom code and Autopilot automates tabular pipelines instead.
options: SageMaker Training Jobs that execute custom user code on managed GPU or CPU compute clusters
SageMaker Autopilot pipelines that automate preprocessing and tuning for tabular business data
SageMaker Debugger hooks that inspect live tensors to catch vanishing gradients during training
JumpStart prebuilt solutions that bundle models, notebooks, and templates for common use cases
q: A company needs a ready-made churn-prediction template with model, notebook, and infrastructure. Where is it?

explain: Stratified k-fold preserves the class ratio in every fold, so rare fraud cases appear in each validation split. Plain random folds can leave some folds with almost no positives.
options: Stratified k-fold, which preserves the class ratio in every fold so rare cases validate reliably
Plain random k-fold, which can leave some folds with almost no rare positives by sampling chance
Single chronological split, which tests one time window but cannot average performance over folds
Training-only resubstitution, which reuses training rows and reports an optimistic biased score
q: Fraud labels are 1% positive. Which cross-validation variant gives reliable validation splits?

explain: The tuning objective should be the validation metric, since it guides Bayesian search toward generalizing configurations. Training loss would reward overfitted hyperparameters.
options: Training loss of each trial, which rewards overfitted settings that memorize the training split
A validation metric such as F1 or RMSE that guides search toward generalizing configurations
Wall-clock time per trial, which favors tiny models regardless of their predictive quality level
Number of hyperparameters tried, which counts search effort instead of measuring model quality
q: When configuring an AMT tuning job, which objective should guide the Bayesian search?

explain: XGBoost handles missing values natively, encodes categoricals, and resists overfitting on tabular data. DeepAR needs time series and BlazingText needs text input.
options: DeepAR forecaster that expects timestamped series and cannot exploit static mixed-type columns
BlazingText embeddings that require raw text documents rather than numeric and categorical rows
XGBoost, which handles missing values and mixed tabular features robustly with little tuning
K-Means clustering that groups unlabeled rows but predicts no supervised target column at all
q: A churn table has missing values and mixed categorical plus numeric columns. Which algorithm is most robust?

explain: A fallback to On-Demand with checkpointing keeps long jobs progressing when Spot capacity vanishes. Depending on Spot alone stalls the project whenever interruptions cluster.
options: Running only On-Demand instances from the start, which avoids interruptions but pays full price always
Disabling checkpoints to save S3 writes, which forces every interrupted Spot job to restart fully
Using a single Spot instance with no retry policy, which stalls training whenever capacity disappears
Managed Spot Training with S3 checkpointing plus an On-Demand fallback queue for long-running jobs
q: A 48-hour distributed job on Spot keeps getting interrupted and restarts from scratch. What design fixes it?

explain: A giant embedding table needs model parallelism while the compute-heavy encoder scales with data parallelism. Pure data parallel fails because no single GPU holds the embeddings.
options: Hybrid parallelism: model-parallel embeddings plus data-parallel encoders synchronized with AllReduce
Pure data parallelism that replicates the whole model on every GPU including the huge embedding table
Single-GPU training with gradient accumulation, which never addresses memory or throughput limits
Model-parallel-only sharding of every layer, which complicates batching without helping throughput
q: A ranking model has a 200 GB embedding table plus heavy encoders. Which distributed design trains it feasibly?

explain: JumpStart fine-tuning adapts a foundation model to domain language with labeled examples and evaluation. Prompt-only use cannot reliably learn niche terminology or be measured.
options: Training a built-in classifier from scratch, which discards language knowledge the foundation model has
JumpStart fine-tuning of a foundation model on labeled domain tickets plus held-out evaluation
Prompting a generic model with no examples, which cannot reliably learn niche support terminology
Keyword rules over ticket text, which miss paraphrases and cannot generalize to new phrasings
q: Support tickets use niche product jargon and need accurate classification. Which JumpStart approach fits best?

explain: Cold-start series lack history, so DeepAR's related-series learning plus categorical features transfers patterns. A per-series ARIMA cannot learn from other products at all.
options: Per-series ARIMA models that fit each product alone and cannot transfer patterns to new items
A global moving average that ignores product attributes and seasonal structure across the catalog
DeepAR trained on related series with categorical product features to transfer patterns to new items
XGBoost on static attributes only, which discards sequential seasonality in the sales histories
q: Hundreds of new products have no sales history but resemble existing ones. How should forecasting handle them?

explain: Autopilot's candidate leaderboard exposes pipelines, metrics, and notebooks so experts can inspect and override. Treating the top candidate as final hides preprocessing and validation choices.
options: Deploying the top candidate blindly, which hides preprocessing choices and validation assumptions
Accepting Autopilot defaults for every dataset, which ignores domain constraints and cost limits
Skipping holdout review because AutoML tuned internally, which confuses tuning scores with generalization
Using Autopilot leaderboards and generated notebooks to inspect, compare, and override top pipelines
q: An expert team uses Autopilot for speed but must keep governance. How should it treat AutoML candidates?

explain: Time-series splits must respect chronology so validation always follows training in time. Random k-fold leaks future observations into training and inflates scores.
options: Time-ordered rolling-origin splits where each validation window strictly follows its training period
Random k-fold shuffling that mixes future observations into training and inflates validation scores
Single split on sorted IDs that tests one cutoff without averaging stability across many windows
Resubstitution scoring on training rows that reports memorization rather than future performance
q: A demand model validated with shuffled k-fold scores well but fails live. Which validation fix applies?

explain: Widening the Bayesian search ranges and budget plus early-stopping bad trials explores better regions efficiently. Narrowing ranges around the current best traps search in a poor area.
options: Narrowing ranges around the current best trial, which traps Bayesian search inside a poor region
Widening search ranges with more budget and median-stopping of clearly poor trials to explore better
Freezing all hyperparameters except one, which prevents the optimizer from finding joint interactions
Restarting identical narrow searches, which repeats the same region without learning from history
q: An AMT job plateaus at mediocre scores with narrow ranges and no early stopping. What improves the search?

explain: Profiler traces showing host-bound data loading call for Pipe mode or more workers, not bigger GPUs. Adding GPUs to a starved pipeline leaves them idle.
options: Adding larger GPUs to the job, which leaves expensive accelerators idle while input starvation persists
Raising batch size blindly, which grows memory pressure without fixing the slow host-side pipeline
Fixing the input pipeline with Pipe mode or more workers, as Profiler shows host-bound data loading
Enabling Debugger tensor rules, which inspect gradients but cannot relieve data-delivery starvation
q: Profiler shows low GPU use with the job bound on data loading from S3. What is the right fix?

explain: Tuning the threshold on validation data using F1 or cost analysis picks the operating point deliberately. Default 0.5 ignores asymmetric costs and class imbalance.
options: Keeping the default 0.5 cutoff, which ignores asymmetric error costs and skewed class prevalence
Maximizing training accuracy, which rewards memorization instead of choosing a live operating point
Picking the threshold by visual guess, which cannot quantify cost trade-offs across operating points
Tuning the threshold on validation data with F1 or cost analysis to match asymmetric error costs
q: Missing fraud costs far more than a false alarm, but the team uses cutoff 0.5. What should it do instead?

explain: The elbow method plots within-cluster sum of squares against K and picks the bend where gains diminish. The silhouette score then confirms separation quality of the chosen K.
options: Setting K equal to the number of rows, which memorizes every record as its own useless cluster
Fixing K at two by default, which imposes an arbitrary split unrelated to the data structure
Elbow analysis of within-cluster variance versus K, confirmed with silhouette separation scores
Maximizing K until metrics rise, which overfits clusters and destroys generalization to new data
q: A team must choose K for customer segmentation with K-Means. Which selection method is sound?

explain: AUC measures ranking quality across thresholds and stays informative under class imbalance, so maximizing validation:auc guides tuning toward models that separate rare fraud from legitimate cases. Error rate and RMSE hide ranking behavior, and training metrics reward memorization.
options: Maximize validation:auc, which ranks positives above negatives without a fixed cutoff
Minimize validation:error, which counts plain misclassifications at a single cutoff
Minimize validation:rmse, which measures squared error of raw regression outputs
Maximize training auc, which rewards scores computed on the same training rows
q: A team tunes SageMaker XGBoost for highly imbalanced fraud detection with Automatic Model Tuning. Which objective metric setup should it use?

explain: Custom containers must expose metrics through MetricDefinitions pairing a Name with a Regex that parses stdout CloudWatch logs, and ObjectiveMetricName must match one of them. Without a matching regex the tuning job reports the objective metric missing.
options: Set the search direction to Maximize in the console and let SageMaker detect the emitted value automatically
Define a MetricDefinition with a regex capturing the number and set it as ObjectiveMetricName
Write the loss only to a local file inside the container since the service reads container files directly
Optimize on instance CPU utilization since resource signals can steer the search toward cheaper trials
q: A custom PyTorch container prints lines like Validation-loss=0.25 to stdout. How should the team make an AMT job tune on that value?

explain: Hyperband uses successive halving to stop underperforming configurations early and spend budget on promising ones. Bayesian optimization is sample-efficient but does not early-stop by itself, while grid search wastes budget on poor regions.
options: Bayesian search alone, which models past trials but always runs each job to completion
Grid search alone, which exhaustively evaluates every combination without early pruning
Hyperband with early stopping, which halts weak configurations and reallocates budget
Manual one-by-one runs, which depend on engineer intuition without systematic pruning
q: A team has budget for 60 training jobs and wants poor trials stopped early to save cost. Which AMT tuning strategy fits best?

explain: Warm start reuses parent tuning history to seed the new search; on new or refreshed input data the correct type is TRANSFER_LEARNING (same algorithm, different data), while IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM requires unchanged input data and image, e.g. to add more jobs.
options: A brand-new random search each week, discarding all previous tuning trial results
Grid search over identical ranges, which repeats past evaluations without transfer
Tuning on training loss only, which reuses logs but pushes search toward overfitting
Warm start tuning with IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM to seed search from parent jobs
q: A team retrains the same XGBoost model weekly on fresh sales data and wants to reuse prior tuning history. What should it configure?

explain: LightGBM uses histogram-based leaf-wise growth that trains faster and uses less memory than XGBoost on very large tabular data while keeping competitive accuracy. DeepAR, K-Means, and vision algorithms target unrelated data modalities.
options: LightGBM built-in, which trains faster with lower memory on very large tabular sets
DeepAR recurrent network, which expects timestamped series rather than static rows
K-Means clustering, which groups unlabeled rows without predicting any target
Semantic Segmentation FCN, which labels every pixel of input images for vision
q: A 10-million-row CSV needs fast low-cost tabular fraud training with minimal accuracy loss. Which built-in algorithm choice is most efficient?

explain: Random Cut Forest builds random partition trees and scores points by how easily they isolate, which suits unsupervised anomaly detection on metrics streams. XGBoost and Linear Learner are supervised and BlazingText targets text.
options: XGBoost classifier, which needs labeled positive and negative training examples
Random Cut Forest, which scores anomalies in streaming numeric data unsupervised
BlazingText classifier, which learns from large labeled text document collections
Linear Learner regressor, which fits linear models to labeled numeric targets
q: A DevOps team must flag anomalous spikes in streaming CPU and latency metrics without labeled examples. Which built-in algorithm fits?

explain: Latent Dirichlet Allocation is the unsupervised SageMaker built-in for topic modeling, assigning documents to latent themes without labels. XGBoost needs labels, DeepAR needs series, and Object Detection works on images.
options: Object Detection SSD, which draws labeled bounding boxes around objects in images
XGBoost classifier, which requires labeled rows for supervised tabular prediction
LDA topic modeling, which discovers latent themes in unlabeled document collections
DeepAR forecaster, which learns seasonal patterns from related time-series streams
q: A publisher must discover hidden themes across 200,000 unlabeled support articles. Which built-in algorithm should it use?

explain: Image Classification predicts a single label per whole image, matching pass-fail inspection without localization. Detection adds boxes and segmentation adds pixel maps, both unnecessary overhead when only an image-level verdict matters.
options: Semantic Segmentation FCN, which assigns a class to every pixel of the image
Object Detection SSD, which predicts bounding boxes plus labels for each object
K-Means clustering, which groups feature vectors without learning defect labels
Image Classification, which assigns one label to each entire input image
q: A factory must label each whole product photo as defective or good, with no location needed. Which built-in algorithm fits?

explain: Object2Vec learns embeddings from pairs such as co-viewed products or sentence pairs, enabling nearest-neighbor similarity and ranking. Linear Learner, DeepAR, and Image Classification address different modalities and do not learn pair-based embeddings.
options: Object2Vec, which learns embeddings from paired items for similarity and ranking
Linear Learner, which fits linear regression on dense tabular numeric features
DeepAR forecaster, which models timestamped demand series with recurrent nets
Image Classification, which assigns one topic label to each whole input image
q: A shop wants product embeddings learned from co-view pairs to power similar-item search. Which built-in algorithm fits best?
source: Adattata da Udemy – practice test MLA-C01

explain: K-Means exposes test:msd measuring mean squared distance to cluster centers, so minimizing it tightens clusters. Accuracy and AUC need ground-truth labels that unsupervised clustering lacks.
options: Maximize validation:auc, which needs binary labels unavailable in clustering
Minimize test:msd, the mean squared distance of points to assigned centers
Maximize validation:accuracy, which counts correct labels missing here
Minimize training loss alone, which AMT forbids as an objective for built-ins
q: A team tunes SageMaker K-Means clustering with AMT. Which objective metric configuration is valid?

explain: Linear Learner is optimized for large-scale linear classification on high-dimensional sparse inputs such as TF-IDF, training faster and cheaper than tree ensembles there. K-Means is unsupervised while DeepAR and segmentation target other modalities.
options: DeepAR recurrent forecaster, which expects ordered timestamped sequences rather than static document vectors
K-Means clustering, which groups unlabeled rows by similarity without ever predicting document labels
Linear Learner, which scales linear models efficiently to high-dimensional sparse data
Semantic Segmentation network, which produces pixel-level label maps for input images instead of text
q: A team classifies documents with 100,000 sparse TF-IDF features and needs fast linear training at scale. Which algorithm should it pick?

explain: Chronos is a pre-trained time-series foundation model that generates forecasts zero-shot for new series with little history and no training job. DeepAR and ARIMA need sufficient history or per-series fitting, while static XGBoost ignores sequence structure.
options: Training DeepAR from scratch, which needs long related histories and GPU hours
Tuning XGBoost on static attributes, which discards sequential seasonal patterns
Fitting per-store ARIMA models, which cannot borrow patterns across locations
Zero-shot Chronos foundation model from JumpStart without task-specific training
q: A retailer needs immediate forecasts for brand-new stores with almost no history and no training budget. Which JumpStart approach fits?

explain: Pipe mode streams records directly from S3 to the training process, avoiding full dataset download, cutting disk use and startup time. Compute or optimizer changes cannot fix storage-bound ingestion.
options: Pipe input mode, which streams S3 data to training without full local download
Larger CPU counts, which add compute but leave disk-full failures unresolved
Higher learning rate, which changes optimization without touching data delivery
Stronger L2 penalty, which constrains weights without fixing input bottlenecks
q: A 500 GB S3 dataset fills training instance disks and delays epoch start with File mode. What should the team change first?

explain: SageMaker syncs /opt/ml/checkpoints to the configured checkpoint S3 URI and restores it when Spot replaces instances, letting training resume instead of restarting. Disabling checkpoints or using ephemeral storage loses progress on every interruption.
options: Disable all checkpoints to save S3 writes and restart faster after each interruption
Write checkpoints to /opt/ml/checkpoints with checkpoint S3 URI for automatic resume
Store checkpoints only in instance RAM so restore avoids any S3 download delay
Keep checkpoints on the driver notebook since training nodes cannot reach S3
q: A Managed Spot Training job must survive interruptions without losing epochs. How should checkpointing be configured?
source: Adattata da Udemy – practice test MLA-C01

explain: Debugger applies built-in rules such as vanishing_gradient, overfit, or loss_not_decreasing to live tensors and emits alerts during the job. Profiler covers hardware utilization while Experiments and Registry handle tracking and governance.
options: SageMaker Experiments lineage, which records datasets and parameters after runs finish
SageMaker Profiler charts, which report GPU use without inspecting gradient values
SageMaker Debugger rules, which evaluate tensors live and flag training pathologies
SageMaker Model Registry, which versions approved models for production release
q: Training loss stalls and the team suspects vanishing gradients or overfitting mid-run. Which SageMaker capability raises automatic alerts?

explain: AMT tunes hyperparameters of a user-defined training setup with fixed code and data pipeline, while Autopilot automates preprocessing plus algorithm search end to end. With preprocessing frozen, AMT is the direct and cheaper fit.
options: Autopilot, because it is the only SageMaker service capable of training XGBoost models at all
Autopilot, because AMT cannot optimize XGBoost hyperparameters and supports only built-in vision algorithms
JumpStart solution, because search jobs cannot run user-chosen algorithms and need prebuilt templates only
AMT, because Autopilot would rebuild preprocessing unnecessarily instead of tuning given setup
q: A team already has a fixed preprocessing pipeline and only wants the best XGBoost hyperparameters. Autopilot or AMT?

explain: R-squared reports explained variance as a ratio, which communicates overall fit in one business-friendly number. MAE, MAPE, and max error describe error scale but not the proportion of variance captured.
options: R-squared, the share of target variance explained by the model predictions
MAE, the average absolute error expressed in original price units across all listings
MAPE, the average percentage gap relative to each actual sale price in the set
Max error, the single largest absolute miss across the full dataset
q: Marketing wants one number showing how much price variance a regression explains. Which metric should lead the report?

explain: MAPE divides each error by its actual, so zero actuals cause division by zero and huge instability. RMSE and MAE measure absolute-scale errors without that division and compare models reliably on sparse demand.
options: Keep MAPE but drop all zero rows, which biases evaluation toward nonzero periods
Use RMSE or MAE, which avoid dividing by zero and stay stable on zeros
Use accuracy, which counts exact matches unsuitable for continuous demand
Use AUC-ROC, which ranks binary labels rather than scoring demand errors
q: Intermittent-demand data contains many zero actuals and MAPE explodes. Which metric swap fixes model comparison?
source: Adattata da Udemy – practice test MLA-C01

explain: Precision-recall AUC concentrates on performance where positives are rare and avoids the flood of true negatives that make ROC look good. For severe imbalance it discriminates models that ROC cannot separate.
options: Accuracy at a fixed 0.5 cutoff, which rewards always predicting the majority class blindly
AUC-ROC alone, which counts many easy negative cases that inflate the overall score
PR-AUC, which focuses on precision-recall tradeoff among rare predicted positives
Training loss, which measures in-sample fit on training rows rather than live ranking quality
q: Fraud is 0.5% of traffic and ROC curves look optimistic for all models. Which metric separates them better?

explain: High and closely aligned train and validation errors signal high bias where the model is too simple to capture signal, and extra data alone does not close it. Adding capacity, features, or training flexibility lowers both errors.
options: Overfitting from excess capacity, fixed by stronger dropout and smaller networks
Label leakage inflating both errors, fixed by removing future features entirely
Time leakage from shuffling, fixed by switching to rolling-origin validation
Underfitting with high bias, fixed by richer features or a more expressive model
q: Learning curves show training error 32% and validation error 34% with more data barely helping. What is the diagnosis and fix?

explain: Shallower trees, higher minimum child weight, L2 penalty lambda, and row or column subsampling all constrain capacity and reduce memorization. The opposite changes grow capacity and widen the train-validation gap.
options: Lower max_depth, raise min_child_weight and lambda, add subsample below 1.0
Raise max_depth, drop min_child_weight, set lambda to zero for full growth
Raise learning rate sharply and remove validation rounds to speed fitting
Train far longer with eta at maximum so trees memorize residual noise
q: XGBoost shows 99% train but 74% validation accuracy. Which hyperparameter change set directly fights this gap?

explain: early_stopping_rounds monitors a validation metric during boosting and halts a trial after a set number of rounds without improvement, keeping the best iteration. Wider ranges or more parallelism do not shorten unproductive trials.
options: Wider eta ranges alone, which expand search without deciding when rounds stop
early_stopping_rounds on a validation set, halting boosting when no gain appears
More boosting rounds fixed for all trials, which extends wasted computation
Higher MaxParallelJobs, which runs more trials but never shortens each trial
q: An XGBoost tuning search wastes rounds long after validation stops improving. Which setting stops that waste inside each trial?

explain: Fitting imputers and scalers before splitting lets validation-fold statistics influence training inputs, producing optimistic CV scores that vanish in production. Preprocessing must fit inside each fold or pipeline step.
options: Too few folds, which only raise score variance without leaking validation information across splits
Too much regularization, which would lower validation scores rather than inflate them upward
Preprocessing leakage, since scalers fitted on all rows leak validation statistics
Excessive tuning budget, which cannot by itself inflate cross-validation estimates
q: A pipeline scales and imputes on the full dataset before cross-validation and reports 97% AUC that collapses live. What is the flaw?

explain: Reusing the same folds for selection and reporting creates selection bias where the best tuning score overestimates true performance. Nested CV isolates tuning in inner loops and estimates generalization on untouched outer folds.
options: Single train-test split, which adds split luck without keeping model choice apart from final scoring
Resubstitution on training rows, which reports memorization instead of future predictive quality
More search jobs on the same partitions, which further push the reported number upward
Nested cross-validation, with inner folds for tuning and outer folds for unbiased scoring
q: A team tunes hyperparameters with regular k-fold and reports the best tuning score as final performance. What evaluation fix applies?

explain: Bayesian optimization picks each batch from completed results, so very wide parallel batches decide trials with stale knowledge and behave more like random search. AMT also never tunes instance type or count, only algorithm hyperparameters.
options: Higher parallelism speeds wall-clock time but weakens Bayesian guidance per trial batch
AMT starts adjusting instance types automatically once parallel job counts grow too high
Objective signals switch to training loss automatically under heavy concurrent load
Warm start history deletes itself whenever concurrent job counts change mid-run
q: An AMT Bayesian job crawls and the team raises MaxParallelJobs sharply to finish sooner. What tradeoff must it accept?
